title: Primer: Using Qubits to Hunt Dark Matter
hook: Wave-like dark matter would jiggle a qubit with a tiny electric field. This free introductory review teaches the whole toolkit — from the Jaynes-Cummings model to the Heisenberg limit — as one story.
key_points: The core mechanism: wave-like dark matter induces an electric field that can excite a qubit.
Dark matter coherence matters, because the signal is a wave with a finite coherence time.
Coupled qubit-cavity dynamics are handled with the Jaynes-Cummings framework.
Noise and decoherence enter through Markovian models described by the Lindblad equation.
Quantum sensing concepts covered include POVMs, the Cramer-Rao bound, the standard quantum limit, and the Heisenberg limit.
Entangled states can push sensitivity past what independent qubits achieve.
content_html: Dark matter searches and quantum computing grew up in different buildings, and the vocabulary shows it. A particle physicist knows what a coherence length of dark matter means; a quantum engineer knows what the Lindblad equation does to a qubit. Detecting wave-like dark matter with qubits requires both at once, and this review is written to close that gap.
extra_html:
Takeo Moroi's introductory review starts from the fundamentals of qubits and the mechanism that makes them detectors at all: wave-like dark matter induces an electric field, and that field can drive a qubit from its ground state to its excited state. Because the dark matter signal is a wave with finite coherence, the review pays close attention to how that coherence shapes the expected excitation rate.

From there it builds the working apparatus. Coupled qubit-cavity systems are treated in the Jaynes-Cummings framework; noise and decoherence come in as Markovian processes described by the Lindblad equation. The last stretch is quantum metrology proper: the operator-sum representation and positive operator-valued measures, the Cramer-Rao bound, the standard quantum limit versus the Heisenberg limit, and how entangled states can buy sensitivity that independent qubits cannot. A useful map if you want to follow — or join — the growing overlap between quantum sensing and the search for physics beyond the Standard Model. Free on arXiv.

related.title: A Quantum Sensor Built to Catch Dark Matter and Ancient Gravitational Waves
related.hook: Two clouds of ultracold atoms, compared against each other, cancel out noise so well that a signal buried in one measurement reappears — aimed at dark matter and ancient gravitational waves.

related.title: Qubits and Quantum Computing
related.hook: A normal bit is a 0 or a 1. A qubit can be both at once — and linking many of them lets a quantum computer explore a staggering number of possibilities together.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

related.title: Don't Measure the Field, Measure the Answer
related.hook: A single-qubit sensor gives you one bit per measurement. Instead of averaging thousands of them into a number, why not spend the quantum processing on the question you actually asked?
